utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, legal intern Marina Marcikic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with Sunna Aevarsdottir, legal intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stringer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 251 which is Exhibit Number P00196.140.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Hadzic, we're going to talk a little bit more about the issue of housing and how the issue of housing was treated and who was handling housing in the SBS [sic] during late 1991 and early 1992? Mr. Hadzic, this is from Dalj on the 2nd of October, 1991, reflecting the session held on that day in Erdut, a decision on the temporary transfer the assets of the Republic of Croatia and socially owned property to the hands of the Serbian district. Do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you -- it appears over your name. Did you, in fact, approve or sign off on this decision in your capacity as prime minister of the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically whether I signed this, but I'm familiar with this. I received these papers when I arrived here. But it's consistent with what I generally remember, to protect private property in some way. But I don't specifically remember whether I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what you just said was interesting to me. You said to protect private property because this decision actually - at least on its face - refers to assets of the Republic of Croatia and socially owned property. My first question is whether this decision would relate to something like an agricultural enterprise, such as the DP Dalj co-operative that we've heard about this in case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I misspoke when I said to protect private property. I meant protecting the property of either the state or a private person. Because from what I remember and from the information I had at the time, the only goal was to protect that property. I was not specifically aware of these things whether it was DP Dalj or some other state-owned company. I just generally supported the idea of protecting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, however, that an enterprise like DP Dalj would fall within the scope of this decision?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for me to agree or not agree with you. I said I was generally in favour of protecting property and this was developed at the level of the ministry. The Ministry of Agriculture. I didn't interfere in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. I think that actually I will ask you to tell me whether or not you agree with me. You've -- you've now referred to the Ministry of Agriculture. We know that the DP Dalj was agricultural enterprise. Was it socially owned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you can see from the name itself. DP, in my language, means socially owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so, in fact, a socially owned company like DP Dalj would fall within the terms of this decision and therefore come into the hands of the Serbian district; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to look at the decision. If you give me a moment. It's clearly written here. In my view, it didn't apply to anything specific. Generally, everything was supposed to be protected and to become the property of the Serbian district.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Including DP Dalj.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. At that moment, that was not my thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not the witness. I'm asking whether you can say it or not, whether you might be willing to agree with me that, in fact, based on the language here, and based on the status of DP Dalj as a social-owned company, DP Dalj was among the socially owned assets that came into the Serbian district, under this decision. Can you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered. At that time, I didn't even know that DP Dalj was a separate specially created company. This applies to everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You didn't know that DP Dalj was a socially owned company in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I didn't know in 1991. I didn't know at the time when this decision was prepared. It was prepared for everything in general. And it was only in the process of being established. It didn't start -- it wasn't up and running immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did housing fall within the terms of this decision as well, the places where people lived?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, but looking at this decision, I believe it was just a temporary transition of the property of the Republic of Croatia and other socially owned property into the property of the Serbian district; whereas housing was a matter of private property. I don't know - at least I don't remember - of any cases of socially owned apartments in the territory where we lived, except, of course, in Vukovar, but Vukovar at this time was not under our control yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it the wish of the SBWS government to take temporary control over housing? For example, to preserve it during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this specific period, but all the decisions that we adopted were exclusively temporary. And the only reason, from the information I had at the time, was to protect property because there was a war going on, there were many people who were outsiders, who were not locals of the area. There were many attempts of robbery and looting, and this was an attempt to prevent looting and robbery. At least that's how it was explained to me. I was not very legally literate in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 250. That's Exhibit 195.140.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, this is also dated the 2nd of October. And it's similar but slightly different from what we just looked at. This is the decree on the temporary protection of abandoned property. And if we look at page 2 of the B/C/S version, it appears to me that -- sorry. Page 3. This document appears over your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if we go back then to Article 1, it says that: "This decree regulates the temporary protection, preservation, and use of property that, in keeping with the decision by the government of the Serbian district on [sic] 2nd October ... became the property of the Serbian District of SBWS, as well as protection, preservation, use of other abandoned property." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Yes, that's what written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in Article 2, it provides that the Ministry of the War-Time Economy is to make a list of the property in Article 1. And then it continues on in the subsequent articles to set out how the process of identifying these properties and managing them is to take place. Now, would you agree with me, Mr. Hadzic, then, that under this decree the SBWS government is asserting authority over housing in the district, that is, abandoned housing, houses of people who are no longer living there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't agree with this phrasing. I can say that it was an attempt by the government to establish its governance. It was a unilateral decision of the government, but there were many other conditions on which this decision and its enforcement depended because the government did not have any influence on the army, the Yugoslav People's Army that was there, and we had no levers of enforcement. This was an attempt to protect the property that was being looted by some people whom I didn't know and who -- whom we were unable to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it also an attempt - and I'm not suggesting necessarily that -- that there's anything wrong about it - at one level, isn't this an attempt simply to regulate managing all of this abandoned housing, keep track of what's there? And then we can look at Article 10. But before we do, just to follow up and ask: Isn't this an attempt by the government to establish a way to regulate and keep track of abandoned housing in the district?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be honest. The government did not have either the wish or the power to control these processes. The only thing we wanted at the time was to protect that property.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Article 8 first because this talks about the Ministry of Justice and Administration shall appoint a commission consisting of at least three members. And as it says here, that commission is to implement the procedure for the protection of property owned by citizens in the liberated territory. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: First question is: Who are the citizens? Serbs and Croats alike, as well as Hungarians, Slovaks, all the other ethnicities living in the district?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it goes without saying that it applies to all citizens. We did not make any distinction by nationality. It means all those who abandoned their property as well as the citizens who remained behind. They were all equal citizens, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Throughout the trial, Mr. Hadzic, we've heard a lot of evidence about non-Serbs who were expelled from the district during late 1991, 1992 and beyond. This decree, it applies to the houses of non-Serbs who were expelled; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot agree with that understanding. I don't see it that way, and what I believe you just said is not correct. This is the 2nd of October, the beginning of a real war, both Serbs and Croats were leaving their houses to flee from the war and, of course, Croats were perhaps leaving in larger numbers, but there were also a lot of Serbs who left for Serbia, some even for Croatia. So this decision dated 2nd of October applies to all citizens. Nobody was driving them out. They were trying to flee from the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you deny that non-Serbs were being driven out of the district by the 2nd of October, 1991? You deny that unequivocally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm neither confirming nor denying. At that time, I was not aware that anyone was being driven out. Anyone who wanted to stay, stayed. Those who wanted to leave were leaving. There was one case later that I heard about in Dalj. Croats had prepared some sort of boat for people who wanted to leave and they took that boat. But the very fact that people were leaving their homes was tragic. But, at that time, I did not have any information that anybody was expelling anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice and Administration that's referred to here in Article 8, that's the ministry whose head was Mr. Susa?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So his job was, then, to appoint this commission of three people who would implement the procedure? Mr. Susa was responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know right now whether it was Susa or not. The Ministry of War-Time Economy was mentioned here. I didn't deal with that at the time, except that I signed this document. And I really cannot tell you now – perhaps it was, I suppose it was, but I am not sure. But he will certainly come here and we'll be able to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in Article 10, it says that: "Property abandoned by citizens may not be transferred to new owners," I'll skip some words, "unless this is done by the owner and is to his advantage." "This may also temporarily be done so as to satisfy the defence needs of the district or when it is in the general interest of the district and its individual parts." Mr. Hadzic, was it under this provision, then, that the government approved Serbs from elsewhere, such as Western Slavonia, to come and to live in the houses abandoned by non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the connection between this decision and the arrival of Serbs from Western Slavonia. I'm not sure I even knew or whether the Serbs from Western Slavonia were already coming at the time. This decision was meant to protect property that was abandoned, and all the legal assumptions mentioned here are something that I see for the first time. I never thought about it, or dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that prior to the conflict Serbs did not constitute a majority in any of the municipalities of your district, it was in the interest of the district to bring in Serbs or to accommodate Serbs from elsewhere inside the district; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not only not true, but it's this kind of thinking that I wouldn't deign to consider if I were not sitting here. At that time, it didn't cross my mind that somebody, some Serbs would come from another territory and move in there and that a Serb majority would be created there. All we wanted was to stay as a part of Yugoslavia. I never thought about that in the least. At least I personally never thought that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before the recess, Mr. Hadzic, and I know it's been several weeks now since we were having this conversation, I showed you a lot of statements, I suggest, in which you were talking about Serbs coming from other parts of Croatia. We don't need to go back all through that again, do we?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the 2nd of October. I don't remember that the Serbs from Croatia had already started arriving at that time. The statements that I was giving were only declarative. You just took my statements out of context and I was only responding to what the Croatian side was saying. And of course, now I'm not a position to show you exactly what I was answering, which Croatian statements. At that time I didn't have the resources or possibility to enforce any of this. I just made political statements. Our territory was in the process of being established, journalists were asking me questions, and I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've said this a few times, Mr. Hadzic, and I want to follow up on it. You just said: "I just made political statements." I think from before you said that your statements about the Western Herzegovinians from the post-World War -- or from the World War II period, those were political statements. You've said this elsewhere as well. What do you mean by that, when you say it's a political statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain it. At that time, Stipe Mesic was a member of the Presidency and he returned from Belgrade once and said: I accomplished my mission. Yugoslavia is no more. And the Serbians who want to leave Croatia but they can take with them only a lump of earth that they brought on their shoes when they had come in the first place. That was also a political statement of sorts, but the difference was that at the time Stipe Mesic, together with Tudjman, controlled the army and had power. It was as a reaction to this that I was making what I call political statements, because I had no means of implementing or enforcing anything, because I did not command any army. I was talking about Western Herzegovinians, and when I say “political,” I should rather say that these were just mere words, declarations. There were many people in my village who were Croats from Bosnia- Herzegovina. One of them even had his son in the Croatian army and still he had no problems. Luka Sutalo was a typical example of those Croats from Western Herzegovina who had come during the war, and I never thought he should be in any trouble because of me. So, when I say “political statements,” I mean that those were empty words. It's perhaps better to put it that way than to call it a political statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So they're things you were saying that you didn't believe at the time personally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was responding to Croatian provocations in the same tone. I was not going around asking people who was born where, in order to have them expelled. Anybody who wanted to stay with us was able to stay. You can see that even now. It's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So when you say "political statements," what you're telling us is that you were saying things that you didn't actually believe yourself. This was just for public consumption?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, why not? You can call it that way. Perhaps a better description would be empty words. Meaningless stories. It's better to call it that way than to call it political statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is your political statements had a profound impact on the events that were taking place at that time; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. First of all, I was giving those political statements in Belgrade and nobody was able to see it in Slavonia and 10 Baranja because there was no electricity and nobody watched the TV programme. Second, the press that published it was not read by anyone in Slavonia and Baranja because no newspapers were available, so people couldn't read newspapers. It was just a political statement for the broader public, Serbian and Croatian, in Serbia and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 2, which is 1D00003.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is an article from Novosti on the 7th of November, 1991, Mr. Hadzic. The title is: "Accommodation Provided." And we can blow this up for you if it would assist you to read the original language version.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the bottom part? This is from the 7th of November. It's more than a month after the document we discussed a couple of minutes ago. And it refers to temporary accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. And so what's happening here, as you've pointed out, this is the 7th of November. A moment ago we were talking about the decrees of the 2nd of October, so this is about a month or so later. Here now you are actually going public and calling upon displaced Serbs to come and temporarily settle in SBWS. You do agree that this is a statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. But it's a humanitarian issue, not a political one. These people had their houses destroyed in Croatia. This is also the territory of Croatia, except it's in the east not the west. Were they people supposed to be without a roof over their heads or were we supposed to give them some temporary accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now here it indicates that according to the statement that was received by this press agency, Tanjug, it said: "Everyone who is interested should apply with the Executive Councils of local communes and the Ministry for Housing, Public Utilities, Reconstruction, temporarily based in Erdut." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, is that how it was actually handled? People who wanted to come into abandoned housing in the SBWS -- or I should say assignment of housing was within the government structures to be handled by Executive Councils and this Ministry for Housing. Is that how it was done?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the process. I neither saw nor heard anybody coming, in response to this invitation, to the ministry in Erdut. I don't even know who made this appeal. And from the evidence you led so far, we saw who established the councils in local communities and who implemented this, bypassing the government. This has nothing to do with the government. We perhaps only tried to put some order into all -- all of this, but nobody addressed the government on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the evidence we led on this was that, for example, in Beli Manastir, it was Mr. Borivoje Zivanovic who was head of the Executive Council, and then later on in SBWS and in the Erdut area actually it was Mr. Ilic. Correct? Those are two of the people we discussed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean the two of them but now I'm going to talk about the two of them. As for what we discussed, that had to do with the Ilok and where the refugees were put in Western Srem, this was done by the JNA. That's what I meant. But now that you mention Mr. Zivanovic and Baranja, you have to know that the municipal assembly in Baranja was established before the government was established. And Zivanovic was president of the municipal executive council, and they had their own laws and regulations and they worked on that basis, apart from the government. And it was only later that Milan Ilic was elected, after the date we are talking about now. I think it was towards the end of 1991 that he was elected president of the municipality of Dalj, and only in the spring of 1992 that he was elected president of the regional government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, when I became the president of the Serb Republic of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have at page 14, line 6, Mr. Hadzic, it indicates -- we see the name "Milovanovic." I wonder whether you were actually referring to Mr. Milan Ilic there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned two names: Boro Zivanovic and Milan Ilic. I just have to look at the context to see whether this is Beli Manastir or Dalj. Yes, yes. This is Milan Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We talked about that before and I don't want go back into that now. But let's talk again about Mr. Zivanovic a little bit and what was happening in his area on assigning of housing. This would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before I do that, Mr. President, I would tender this exhibit, which is 1D00003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, again, this is tab 225, P02163.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As this is coming up, Mr. Hadzic, I can just tell you, this is a decision over -- this is from the Beli Manastir Gazette. It's a decision of Borivoje Zivanovic on appointing a commission to assign flats, houses for temporary use. Now, it's item number 66 in the -- in the gazette, I believe. Now, what you've just said, Mr. Hadzic, I'll agree with you, Mr. Zivanovic was a little bit ahead of the curve, as we say in my language. He was taking this authority early on, this is 14th of September, 1991, even before the SBWS government was officially in existence; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it was only subsequent, later, I think it was in November in which he was appointed to be the head of the Executive Council for Beli Manastir. We looked at that decision before.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was confirmed by the government then but he was already that he been elected by the Municipal Assembly of Beli Manastir, independently of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so then can we agree that, in fact, Mr. Borivoje Zivanovic and his people, this commission here that he is appointing, are handling the issue of housing and assigning housing in Beli Manastir? That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree or disagree with what I see but I'm here to be a witness about the things that I took part in and that happened and that I knew about. I didn't know about any of this. Nobody informed me about this, and I never received a copy of any Official Gazette of the Beli Manastir municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There was no significant JNA or military role in Beli Manastir, right, as opposed, say, to Western Srem? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, could you look on your screen whether we have the decision -- whether this document is the decision we are talking about now? Because this is about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. Yes, what we're seeing on the English actually begins at the bottom of this page, 66. It's item 66 there which, unfortunately, it appears we do not have page 2. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is what I have, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, my last question was whether, in fact, there was no significant JNA or military role in Beli Manastir as opposed to Western Srem. What I mean by that is that the local authorities in Beli Manastir had a great deal more authority and control because, really, there was not much of a conflict that occurred there. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any influence over developments in Beli Manastir. And at that time, I wasn't informed about what was going on, so I don't know how things went in Baranja. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You don't know how things went in Baranja in September and October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Not September and October. You asked about when the army was there and when there were conflicts there. I think that was before that. So I don't know how long the army stayed on and what the situation was like and ... Because these things happened there without me knowing about this. People were saying, by way of a joke, that there was a three-day war in Baranja, but it was short. The army was there, there was always this tension. There was always the possibility of the Croats relaunching ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When was this three-day war, as best as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- well, now I really don't know precisely. But maybe August, beginning of September. But I think it was August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. And so by September, which is when this decision is issued, we can agree, can't we, that the local authorities, Mr. Zivanovic, the local civilian authorities, were in control of and able to exercise their government functions in Beli Manastir; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem that way on the basis of these papers, but I'm not sure that they could have done this on their own without coordinating with the JNA. Because there was still a war situation there and the JNA was there, throughout the territory. And I know that they had very close relations with the JNA, specifically Zivanovic and all of these other people who later showed up in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1476, P1707.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now here we're going to move forward to the 11th of December, 1991, although we're staying with the issue of abandoned property. This is a document of the 1st Military District Command on resolving a request for use of abandoned property. And it's referring to requests from certain local officials for making use of abandoned properties and farms. And in paragraph 1, what's ordered here is that: "All such issues should be resolved in co-operation with and at the request of government officials of SO Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem ... followed by officials selected by the SO, which is the Serbian district government as well as Serbian district government recognised local organs or [sic] authority." And so by the 11th of December, what we're seeing throughout the area of the 1st Military District, their area of responsibility, is co-operation with local authorities in respect of housing and abandoned housing, in particular; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In item 3, because the JNA did not want to be associated with issues involving possible abuse of abandoned property, it is also ordered that local authorities are in charge of managing locally abandoned properties and it's their obligation to create records, et cetera. And it continues to talk about the role envisioned by the local authorities in making and keeping of records, et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving down to item 6: "Local commands shall honour the municipal assembly decisions, Executive Council decisions, and decisions made by the government of SO Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem regarding handing over, that is, using abandoned properties." So what we see in the evidence, Mr. Hadzic, is, in fact, local authorities and local legislation, district legislation asserting control over the issue while, at the same time, we see the JNA quite keen on co-operating with and ceding this issue to the local authorities. That's really how it was, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that's not right. And I think that you know that. What we can see here is that the army is just speaking about this by way of declarations. You have several examples but I'll take only one, say, Ilok. They didn't even want to talk to us before UNPROFOR came. There was military government there. And we see here -- you say "local government." No, we see that it's the military that is in charge of everything here and that the Town Commands decide on everything and they may accept some decision of the local government. They just put this on paper. This is not what you're trying to prove or what you're trying to say. It's the exact opposite. It was Town Commands that did everything on their own. I wrote about Ilok, and I asked them to tell us at least what they took in terms of the socially owned enterprises, cars, accommodation of refugees. They didn't even want to deal with that, talking to us. Up until March, April, they only had military administration there. And they were doing that everywhere. As for this, I don't know who they were lying to. I mean, they never really sent these papers to us. We never knew about this. This was their internal communication. I'm not even sure that it happened at the time. But this proves what I've been saying, not what you've been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about Ilok then. What you've just said is that the Town Commands decide on everything, they may accept some. You say that "they didn't even want to talk to us before UNPROFOR came." That's at line 10 of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to tab 1486, which is P1709.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In fact, there were talks, Mr. Hadzic. What you said just now is not true. There were talks. The JNA was trying to speak to your people, work with your people on this issue in Ilok. This is letter coming from your justice minister, Mr. Susa, from Ilok, on the 29th of December, talking about the commission for organisation and conduct on the operation of moving in and temporary accommodation. So, in fact, Mr. Hadzic, it would appear that Mr. Susa is acting in the capacity that was envisaged under Article 8, I believe it was, of that decree on abandoned property that we were looking at a few minutes ago, referring to the government's commission. As he says: With the aim to ensure better co-ordination has convened a session to be held 30 December at the castle in Ilok with representatives of the Executive Council of Vukovar municipality and all settlements in which temporary accommodation is being carried out. Now, Executive Council of Vukovar municipality, do you recall whether Mr. Miroljub Vujovic, who had been the TO commander on the 20th of November, whether he was still on the Executive Council of the Vukovar municipality at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was the president of the Executive Board that made these appointments. But I have to respond to what you said at first, that I said something that was not correct. No, I'm speaking under oath and everything I said was correct. When I said that they didn't want to talk to us, I meant in practical terms. I mean they did speak to us formally but to return cars to us. They didn't even want to talk about it. Or, rather, they didn't want to return them, but they could have formally discussed this for 100 years but they didn't want to do anything that we proposed. And it is that sense that I said that they didn't want to talk or discuss things because they didn't want to do anything for us. And that is why I said that. They just kept on talking and talking but meaninglessly and that's what I meant. Everything I said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And attached to this letter, this invitation, if I can put it that way, just to -- to finish that off, Mr. Susa says: "We believe that your presence would contribute to, first of all, better detection of problems and ways of resolving them," et cetera. So he is inviting this colonel to a meeting at Ilok to discuss housing. And then he attaches to this letter a lot of data and I want to ask you about some of the data that's attached to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in that, Mr. President, we're going to have to work with the B/C/S version because the English version doesn't -- it has the tables but it really doesn't contain all the data. And so just to go to page 2 of this in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What this is, Mr. Hadzic, can we agree, is a list of the residents of Vinkovci and Vukovar municipalities according to the census, 1991 census. Do you see that at the top?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written here. But I do apologise to you, I don't know what the context is. I mean, what you read, Susa's letter. Susa was only for Ilok, and this is for the entire municipality of Vinkovci and Vukovar. And I don't think that Susa was the one who drew this up, if that is what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The data that's reflected on here - and I know there's a lot - but what it does is to set out the composition of the population in various settlements. Is that a correct way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so we can see a lot of the settlements are virtually entirely Croat. 99 per cent, 97, 100 per cent. And then, of course, other settlements have different compositions.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I just have to point something out. I would like you to know something. This is the territory of the entire municipality of Vinkovci. More than half of this territory was not within the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now if we could go to page with the ERN number of the B/C/S version it's the page ending with 8953. Right now we're at 8942 so we need to move down about 11 pages. So we're going to skip over. 8953. In the English, it's page -- in e-court, page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this has a table. And what we're seeing on this page, and the names are written in the Cyrillic text on the left-hand column, number 2, but let's take, for example, item number 27, Tovarnik. Is that Tovarnik we're seeing there in row number 27?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tovarnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving from left to right, we've got a series of columns that relate to where it says at the top "pre rata" that's before the conflict. And then the next set of columns, "posle rata," that's post-conflict or war. Isn't that true, that's what that means?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written there, but I don't know who drew up this table. I still don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is this a document of the JNA? It's come to us from the Serbian -- we can see from the stamp, it's coming from the Serbian Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that you got that, but I'm just saying that I did not discuss that and none of the government members drew this up. I cannot testify about it here. I can just give my opinion here, as if I were some kind of expert, but otherwise I cannot testify about it. I've never actually seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What I want to do is to go with you through some of the figures that are set out here. Because, for example, staying with Tovarnik, what we see before the war, pre-war, is that 2050 Croats lived there, or 69 per cent of the population; 890 Serbs, or about 30 per cent. And then post-conflict we see about the same number of Serbs, 880, but now the number of Croats has dropped from 2050 to 150. In other words, the majority has now become a minority down to 36.5 per cent. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. The Croat majority left with the Croatian army when the JNA came.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we can agree to disagree about the reasons why the Croatian community left. If we can move out six more columns to the right, out to column number 15. Now, are you able to tell what you say this column refers to? This refers to whether there's a local government. Correct? Has government been formed, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA wrote "da," "yes," in Cyrillic there. I can only translate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so -- well, looking at row number 26 which is for Boksic, here it indicates that there is not a local government but that for the other places there is; such as Tovarnik. Indicates there is a local government here. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it says "no," "ne" Boksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then if we go to the next page, these are more places. Number 16 is Ovcara; 17 is Sotin, for example. Sotin, we see that the composition of this place went from 62 per cent Croat pre-war to 9 per cent Croat post-conflict. We see there that the Serbian population in Sotin went from 363 people pre-conflict up to 786 people or 86 per cent of the population there post-conflict. And we're not going to go through all of these, Mr. Hadzic, but what's happening here, isn't it, is that we're seeing Croats out and Serbs in, the number of Serbs in many of these villages increasing significantly, thus establishing Serbian majorities in what had previously been Croat-majority villages and towns. Isn't that what this shows?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I don't know anything about this table. That's what it shows. Now, whether this is correct, I don't know. I have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But what we're seeing here is a reflection of what you were advocating in the newspaper article that we just looked at, for example, that Serbs from other places, including displaced Serbs - and, of course, we don't dispute that Serbs were being displaced in large numbers from Western Slavonia - but in any event, Serbs from elsewhere are coming in and they're moving into these places in which the Croats and other non-Serbs used to live. This is just a reflection of what's happening, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I invited them to come in and move temporarily. I had the experience of my own village where were there only Serbs. People moved into Serb houses, not only Croat houses, so it wasn't only Croat houses, but these people had to be put up somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, again, on this page, if we move out to column number 15, the question on has government been formed, yes or no, here we see that a government's been formed in all these places; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise, it was the authority established by the Yugoslav People's Army, as you probably know, and the Trial Chamber now knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving to the next page, which ends with the ERN number 8955, we see a number of the places that we're all more familiar with in this trial in the Western Srem region. Row number 1, we see Ilok; 4.000 Croats down to 850. 54 per cent of the population down to 13.7. Sarengrad. Bapska, 1711 Croats now down to 400. 97 per cent of the population down to 43. Mohovo, Opatovac, Lovas, similar. Lovas, 91.9 per cent Croat now post-conflict is, or post-war, down to 12.3 per cent. And again, Mr. Hadzic, for all these places we see that there is a local -- I should say, that a government has been formed. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's these governments that we're seeing that are handling the issue of housing, accommodating the Serbs, assigning the housing to the incoming Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can only suppose because I had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1488, P1710.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just the previous exhibit started with that letter from Mr. Susa to the colonel inviting them to the meeting in Ilok to talk about housing on the 30th of December. Now this exhibit is dated the following day, 31st of December. Report on the government session, and this is directed to the 1st Military District Command, civilian affairs. And here the person writing this whose name is Milos Miljovic, assistant commander for civil affairs, he refers to the meeting in the first paragraph of the commission for populating and temporary accommodation. And then second paragraph he says that the meeting was attended by Deputy Prime Minister Bogunovic. Is that Boro Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Minister for Justice and Administration, Vojin Susa. Member of the Executive Council, municipality, Milorad Visic. Representatives of TO and Executive Councils of the majority of the local communes of the places that are listed. And then it continues to say that Mr. Susa opened the meeting by presenting its goal in the introduction. It says that: "A large number of refugees did not come at the invitation of the government but in an unorganised manner and that it is our duty to receive them and secure accommodation for them in a more organised manner than so far. He said the government appointed a group led by deputy prime minister." Now, again, the reference to the deputy prime minister here, is that going to be Mr. Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then continuing on the next page: Bogunovic who will deal with this coming task to set up accurate records of temporarily populated persons and solve the issues of food and medical. And then continuing at the end of paragraph: "He says that the Executive Council of Vukovar has been set up and functioning and that in the future it would co-ordinate these actions, although at this stage it had to focus on Vukovar itself." So, in fact, Mr. Hadzic, what we see is by the end of December certainly, your government is actively engaged in the issue of managing the housing, accommodating incoming Serbs, and taking control over the issue, keeping records, et cetera, dealing with food and medical. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not define that properly. We don't see that our government was involved on the 30th of December. On the 30th of December, our government was trying to get involved. This was a first meeting, a first contact, and by that time the JNA had finished everything. Our first contact was when everything was already over. That was our attempt to get involved and to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just skipping down a couple of paragraphs, I'd like to ask you about what the government was trying to do. Deputy prime minister said: "We do not know what our goals are here. We want the structure here to change. Some people do not understand military administration well?" And the person writing this report says that: "These quotes illustrate that the government wants to change the structure of the population at all costs, even by pushing them under the impact of artillery in the zone of intense combat activities, while we do not know what our goal is, can mean that why doesn't the army free the whole of Slavonia and hand us over authority on a plate. His support of immigration even in the zone of intense combat activities did not cease even after the warning by a representative of the division command that we did not recommend populating refugees to the west of Tovarnik to spare them from experiencing exodus twice." So, Mr. Hadzic, if people in the JNA were hesitating on turning over, giving free rein to your government people on the issue of housing, it's because, as they concluded, your government didn't actually care about the safety of the people it wanted to bring in, you only cared about changing the ethnic composition. That's what's being said here, isn't it, and that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was, one. And second, this was written by an organ of the institution which cleansed Croats from Ilok. They did all that. And he is writing here, and you are taking him at his word and you are believing this institution in this case, although in other cases, of course, they were not to be believed. And we have two Prosecution witnesses here, one was not protected, that's Boro Bogunovic, and you could have asked him. And the second one, who did all this, was protected, so I'm not going to mention his name. And now I'm supposed to talk about events of the 30th of December when all that was already over and when we got involved for the first time. And I'm supposed to believe a colonel of the JNA, the institution which did all that, and to take the blame for it too. As for myself, I can really say I know nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to put it to you, sir, that this report was written by a gentleman who has absolutely no reason to lie in his reporting to his superiors about the content of the meeting, and he makes it quite clear that the concerns that they have regarding the safety of the Serbian population that your government is so desperate to put into these areas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm testifying here, and I can only say what I know. Colonel Belic wrote me a letter in a decent tone but very indecently accusing me that we had done nothing for the refugees, that we had not established the boards that he thought we were supposed to set up, and that we basically did nothing. And now some other colonel, based on all that was done - and we all know what was done, we know who did it in Ilok, in what way, we know everything - now this man is trying to say that Boro Bogunovic made some statement and we don't even see that Boro said it. Instead, this colonel is giving us his conclusions about Boro -- about what Boro thought about sending people to the front line. Well, it wasn't us who were sending the people. The people came themselves, and they went where they wanted. We could not send them by a directive. When I say "we," I mean the government, and not even the JNA could do that. So as for the resettlement in some peripheral areas, first of all, the government had nothing do with it. We were surprised by what had happened in Ilok, but no one dealt specifically with any peripheral areas. And as for what this colonel said, I don't believe him, and if you want to believe him, you are free to do so. I think we should have asked your witness Bogunovic about this. But when Susa comes, we'll ask him, as I was not present at that meeting. I don't see from this that Boro Bogunovic said that people should be resettled at any cost in peripheral areas, to be cannon fodder. That's the conclusion of this man, this colonel. But in my eyes, he is neither an honourable man nor an honest man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you say he is neither honourable or honest, are you talking about the person that wrote this report, Mr. Milos Miljovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean him. I don't know him personally, that was the first time I heard of him, but I believe the conclusion he is making here is completely incorrect. I have no reason to defend Boro Bogunovic here, but nowhere in this text do I see that he wanted to send people as cannon- fodder somewhere. That was this man's conclusion. Maybe I'm wrong. Maybe I didn't read it very well but I can -- I can read it more carefully now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, it was the policy of the government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, it is more or less that time -- well, no, not more or less, it is. Would it be convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn for 30 minutes. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, at the beginning of the hearing this morning, I omitted to remind you that you are still under oath, but I'm sure you know, you realise that, as long as you are in this chair, you are under oath and rules being set out stay in force. Thank you. Mr. Stringer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have tab 1481, which is Exhibit D30. 00030.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just before the break, I believe you referred to an exchange of correspondence that you had with Colonel Belic of the Ilok Town Command and so it seemed a good opportunity to discuss this exchange of letters briefly, which I'd like to do now. And the first of these, which is your letter to him, should be coming up. Do you see that there? Do you recognise that as your letter to Colonel Belic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because -- and you can correct me if I'm wrong, but throughout your testimony this morning you've been telling us, I believe, that you really weren't involved and you didn't have any knowledge or involvement on the issue of housing. Here we see that actually as of the 23rd of December at least you're becoming directly involved in your capacity as prime minister. So you were informed of what was happening and you did participate in dealings with the JNA on this issue. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to explain this because you drew a conclusion that I thought impossible to draw. When I said I didn't deal with this, I meant the period around the events in Ilok, because at that time these processes had almost finished already. It is common knowledge when I began to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would suggest that Mr. Hadzic repeat his question [sic] because the considerable and the significant part of it was not transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, repeat his question or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not question, sorry. His answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer -- oh, his answer, okay. Mr. Hadzic, could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to paraphrase because I can't repeat it exactly as the first time. I didn't expect that you would draw the conclusion that you drew because I thought I was quite clear when I said that we didn't deal with it, meaning the government, namely, the resettlement in Ilok. We were not involved when the process was under way. I believe it's common knowledge and we see from this date that I only started dealing with it and heard about it towards the end of 1991, in late December 1991, when all this had already been finished. We were trying to establish civilian authorities there, but even then we were not allowed to. And as I already said today, the military government in Ilok lasted until the beginning of 1992 and the arrival of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So can we agree, then, by the end of 1991, you and your government was -- were directly involved then on the issue of housing and accommodation and that you acquired greater responsibility on that issue as time went on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot agree. Because it was only towards the end of 1991 that we tried to get involved, but since there was a military government, they didn't let us and they appointed all the civilian officials there, including directors of enterprises in Ilok, and we had very little influence on it. At the beginning, almost none. In fact, I don't know that we had any influence at that time. I really believe we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On page 2 of your letter here, third paragraph in the English, you say: "In an effort to eliminate or at least reduce possible problems from our side we have appointed the minister of justice, Mr. Susa, as our representative ..." So then this being the 23rd of December, we were just before the break talking about the meeting that Mr. Susa had with them on the 30th of December. So when Mr. Susa was meeting -- when Mr. Susa, Mr. Bogunovic were meeting with the JNA on the 30th of December, it was pursuant to the appointment that you have referred to here in your letter; correct? He has been given this responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe there's an --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed the error in translation in the paragraph just read by Mr. Stringer. Because the original should be "in an effort to influence on elimination," not "in an effort to eliminate." [Interpretation] I will read out from the original. "Wishing to exert our influence to eliminate or at least reduce possible problems."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's in the record. I think to the extent that there may be any difference, I don't think it requires any further clarification, unless Your Honours would like some.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The point -- my point, Mr. Hadzic, is what's indicated here, you, your government has appointed Mr. Susa to take this responsibility, and that's what he was doing then the following week on the 30th when he met with the JNA to talk about the housing situation in Ilok; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was our attempt to have some influence, if possible, to help, but the attempt came late, because all this had already been finished by the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you go on to talk about how you're hoping anyway to get your minister of finance involved, giving him - this is skipping down a paragraph - "an opportunity to check the situation and flow of funds on transfer accounts ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to find it, but I remember. That seems to have been the main problem for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then on page 3 of the English, and this is skipping down about four more paragraphs, it says: "The government has been told that the settling of Ilok went on rather well." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you say: "We would appreciate at least being informed about the criteria according to which it was done, with the possible remark that our approval does not go without saying." And then after that you say: "This all the more in view of your request, which represents a novelty as conveyed by Mr. Susa, that a reason must be stated and approval given for temporary settlement of refugees in settlements around Ilok." Now, I'm going to suggest to you, Mr. Hadzic, that among the reasons why the JNA wanted to retain some level of control over this was because you, your government, and its representatives were intent on placing Serbs throughout these territories without regard to their own safety and in areas that were still in the conflict zone as was indicated in the previous exhibit we looked at.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I said it in my answer before the break. Maybe I don't have the right to ask and it's not courteous but from what did you get this conclusion? I couldn't see that in this at all, and I couldn't even suppose. It's not written anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hadzic, I think we draw different interpretations of the exhibit that we were looking at before the break. I don't intend to go back to it unless the Chamber would like to revisit it, the language. Skipping down two more paragraphs, there's a reference here in your letter to a report submitted to the government by Mr. Susa and Mr. Bogunovic, Deputy Prime Minister. And, again, just to confirm, Mr. Bogunovic then had by this point been appointed by you also to join Mr. Susa in these discussions with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Him and Mr. Bogdan Vojnovic, who was minister of finance. It was a three-member commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now the next document is tab 1484, which is the letter that came in response from Colonel Belic. This is P1962, dated the 25th of December. And at the beginning he greets you and says it his pleasure to establish official mutually beneficial contact with you. Moving down to the bottom of page 1 of the English, which is the fourth paragraph after this one, he says: "I must admit that I expected there be would be comprehensive, primarily planned and organised involvement by members of the government of SBWS in connection with the settlement of refugees from Western Slavonia." I'm going to skip down a few lines. He says: "I'm disappointed to have to say and inform you that the people you entrusted with the resolution of the most important civilian matter at the moment have not demonstrated any shred of the necessary skills, resourcefulness, knowledge, and, most devastating of all, good will. Naturally, it is difficult to deceive people who have suffered and lay the blame on others, and I say this because we have heard many serious criticisms of your government from many people." So again, Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to put it to you that despite all your complaints about the military rule and the JNA, the role of the JNA on this issue particularly in the Ilok area, the JNA took on this role because the government had, so far, failed to establish or show that it was willing or able to do so itself. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was indicted before this Honourable Court for the events referred to in the indictment. One is that I was involved in the forced expulsions and resettlement of these area by Serbs. It's clear from this letter that the colonel is accusing me of not having done that and this should be, in fact, a crucial Defence exhibit proving that the charges in the indictment are untrue. I'm now explaining something that you are all able to see, that I was not involved in the resettlement of Ilok. I was perhaps a bad president, but it's up to the assembly to discuss it. But if what Mr. Belic says and what Mr. Prosecutor says is true, then I can't be charged with it because I did not lend any attention to it. What am I supposed to answer to your question? Right, I as the prime minister did not deal with the problems of Ilok. I was not involved in the resettlement of people and Colonel Belic is accusing me of not having done that. I don't think this calls for a legal expert. This is basics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He continues on the next page, page 3 of the English, first full paragraph. This is five paragraphs down in the B/C/S: "I'm saddened by the fact that the problem of settling of people is overshadowed by a request for accommodation to a ministry with a sizeable staff -- with a sizable and staff as yet not approved by you, and the priority task is to find accommodation for their family members." So, really, Mr. Hadzic, at this point, again the JNA has expressed its disappointment at your government's lack of concern for the Serbian people that it wanted to put out into the conflict zone. Now they're expressing their disappointment at your government for this sort of self-interest in getting themselves situated in the nice, beautiful confines of Ilok. True? Everybody has been to Ilok. Everybody knows how beautiful the area is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The page was changed for me only now. Could you please indicate to me which paragraph this is so that I can read it again in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the paragraph that begins with the words: "I am saddened by the fact that ..."

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I see it. Thank you. Well, in your question, again, you mentioned the confrontation line, the front line, and, again, I cannot find that in this text. As for this other thing that is in the text and that I can speak about, proves that this -- that our government did not have any influence over the settlements in Ilok. I mean, we didn't even find accommodation for the three members of the government itself. By the way, two of them were refugees. Susa was a refugee from Vinkovci and there was no place for him and his family to stay, just as it was the case with the people from Western Slavonia. And Bogdan Vojinovic is from Vukovar, but his house had been destroyed, so he had nowhere to stay either, so this supports everything that I've already said. And I can't see – could you show me this reference, if there is one, about resettling people on the frontline, because we didn't discuss resettlement at all. We just sought accommodation for the people who were supposed to be stationed somewhere in Ilok, they had to do something. We did not ask for castles or any particularly beautiful accommodation. We just needed accommodation for them so that they could work and live somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1600. Exhibit65 ter 6527.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, these are the minutes of the meeting of the Serbian District SBWS District Council, the 25th of May, 1992, now. So about five months or so later. This is in Erdut. I want to stay with this document on the issue of the priority of the SBWS and its policy on resettlement even as of late May 1992. Mr. Milan Ilic, he was the head of the SBWS District Council at this point in time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation I received was "oblasni odbor." At the time, Milan Ilic was the prime minister in the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem which remained after me, and I didn't have any contact with them with regard to their work. After me, they were an independent body in relation to the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that is to say, myself, so I really don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, they were a body, they operated under the structure of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, did they not? They were not wholly independent?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the government? Well, I don't know. I had no relationship with them and they probably had communication with the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina. However, they had their regional assembly. They had a high level of autonomy, so they operated through the assembly and the assembly was above them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before the summer recess we looked at the document in which you appointed Milan Ilic, I believe, at that time to be the head of the Executive Council for Erdut. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that, but not Erdut but Dalj. The name of the municipality was Dalj then, and now according to the new Croatian law it was moved to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then we see some other names of persons present at this meeting. Do you know who Pajo Nedic was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, he was in the government. He was minister of industry, I think, that what's it was called, in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And later on he was elected to this District Council but I did not have any particular contact with him after that, and I don't know which exact position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in this document, we see item 2, which is what I wanted to direct your attention to: "President Milan Ilic informed those present about the fact that several villages in the area of the district are virtually uninhabited, and that there's a possibility for populating many other places as well. The great importance of populating these places needs no further elaboration. What needs to be done is take urgent measures for this to take place." And then it continues on as to how to achieve that. Now, Mr. Hadzic, what Mr. Ilic is saying here is that -- or I'm going to put it to you the great importance of populating these areas lies in populating these areas with Serbs so that the Serbian demographic majority that has now been achieved in these areas by this point in time can be maintained. That's the great importance to Mr. Ilic. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not true. I did not attend that meeting. I just have to point something out in response to your previous question. The government confirmed the appointment of Ilic as president of the municipality of Dalj but it was not their proposal, it was the proposal of the local communes. Perhaps I should explain this. Perhaps you really did not understand this. I think that this is accidental and I don't think that it's a major mistake. This was the problem. I know that Slavonia and Baranja are agricultural land. These were abandoned areas. The land was not being tilled. So these were peasants who were living and the land need to be tilled. And I really don't know what Milan Ilic meant but I don't see anything here saying that he had said that it was a particular ethnic group that was supposed to populate the areas. These were villages that had been abandoned, land that had been abandoned, and the land was supposed to be tilled so that there wouldn't be diseases, infections and so on. And someone was supposed to do that there. That's how I understood it and, I mean, that's how it was in political terms. And I don't see where you get this conclusion that it was supposed to be the Serbs and I don't see where he could have brought these people from. And I as president of the republic and of the Krajina, I don't remember having discussed that problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we saw on all the demographic data, the numbers attached to the document earlier this morning, that certainly in so many of these areas where there had been Croatian majorities, those majorities no longer existed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've discussed that before the break. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm asking you: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that I remember we discussed it before the break. Sorry, I guess you didn't understand what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My point is that it was the government's policy - and that's what's being expressed here and in other documents we're going to look at - it was the government's policy to maintain those majorities even those -- I should say Serbian majorities, even though such majorities never existed prior to the conflict. That was the policy and the aim. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not true. I explained concretely what the aim was. It wasn't that some elections were being prepared here between the Serbs and the Croats and that policy was to have as many Serbs as possible to vote. Quite simply, somebody was supposed to live in that village and till the land. Now, the Serbs were the Serbs who were there. We couldn't have brought them from Mars in order to create some kind of majority. The land had to be tilled. There was the problem of disease, infections. There were different problems in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But here we are in May, the 25th of May, 1992, in fact, the people that should have been coming back in to till the land were the Croats who had owned the land and who had lived there before. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told that I did not attend that meeting. I don't know anything about that document. Somebody was supposed to go back there and till that land. Now whether it's going to be Croats who would accept to return or whether it would be Serbs, this is the first time I'm discussing this. I never discussed it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, under the Vance Plan, which you agreed to, wasn't it under the Vance Plan that, in fact, those Croats who were no longer there were to come back? Return of refugees, right? That's what was supposed to happen.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was supposed to be. The Vance Plan was supposed to be carried out. But we were the party that just accepted it, we didn't sign it. We were only notified about it. We did not decide about that. This was between the UN and the -- and Serbia and Croatia. In May, nobody asked us a thing. Not the international community, not Serbia, not Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you don't think that Mr. Ilic here is referring to populating these areas with Croats, do you? I mean, you don't seriously contend that that's what he wants, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot think either one thing or the other. It would not be serious for me to interpret now what he meant. I really don't know. For me it would be logical that Croats who would agree to return to our areas and accept our laws should be welcome. That would be fine with me. It's only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we tender this exhibit 65 ter 6527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because the witness did not give any information. He was not familiar with this document and with this particular meeting. So I -- I believe there is no foundation for admitting of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you were looking at the original. Can we look at page 2 of it. Can you identify the signature that appears at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that "Milan Ilic" is typewritten but I don't know his signature at all. So this signature doesn't say a thing to me. Although I know the Cyrillic alphabet very well, I cannot even tell whether this is Cyrillic or Latin, and I cannot discern what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just a small detour here, Mr. Hadzic, before we move on. I'm looking at your testimony on the 9th of July in this trial. You were actually talking about a conversation you had with Radovan Stojicic about Mr. Bogunovic. This is at page 9594. You testified that Badza, Stojicic, had indicated to you that they didn't want to work with Mr. Bogunovic as minister of interior. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah. And that it was as a result of that that he was removed from that position. I can read -- let me read your answer and then that may make it easier for you. You said: "He didn't" -- this is page 9595. This is what you said,

utterances.speaker: MR. HADZIC
utterances.text: "He didn't tell me: Remove Boro Bogunovic. He told me: Do as you will. However, if Bogunovic remains minister, we will not co-operate with him. At least that's how I understood him." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that, the conversation with Badza, and I remember having testified about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then also on the same page of your testimony, you said that: "Boro was not professional. He didn't have any experience. When we set up the government, he was like an interim solution to the problem that we had. That was the most important thing. He was just not professional enough. He did not have the required knowledge." That's at page 9595. Do you recall having said those words, or words to that effect, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then on the next page you describe then giving this information to Mr. Bogunovic because you said he was your friend. And then you said, this is page 9596: "Badza -- and I said: Badza represents Belgrade, and this is the position of Belgrade. And I see that somehow he agreed to be deputy prime minister rather than minister of police." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I said that Badza was the representative of Belgrade or the representative of this Belgrade police, Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could please have tab 355, which is P197.140.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
