utterances.text: I just want to put a time-frame on this, Mr. Hadzic. These are minutes of the SBWS government meeting on the 29th of November, 1991. And at the meeting we see yourself, we see Stevo Bogic, we see Mr. Bogunovic, Borislav Bogunovic, other members of the government. And then also present we see -- it should say, yes, the session was also attended by Milorad Trosic, Milos Vojnovic, Predrag Radlovic, Milan Milanovic, and then Radovan Stojicic. So Badza was also present at this meeting. And then on page 2 of the English and I believe it's, yes, page 2 also of the B/C/S. Item number 2 just at the bottom of that paragraph it says -- well, it starts off, Mr. Trosic, district public prosecutor, was talking about the situation in terms of crime. There's a discussion about that and then at the end it says: "The discussion also touched upon the matter of appointing the minister of the interior as one of the deputy prime ministers. No particular decisions were adopted with regard to the report." I think that's a report, the report of Mr. Trosic. So does this indicate for us, Mr. Hadzic, roughly the time-frame of your discussion with Badza, his complaint about Mr. Bogunovic, and then the time when Mr. Bogunovic went from being minister of interior to being deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm that with any certainty now because this process regarding the replacement of Bogunovic, it didn't take only a day or two. Perhaps it was a couple of weeks. So around that date, yes, but probably these talks took place before that. It's not that Boro agreed immediately. So this was a time of persuasion. I don't know whether it was ten days, 15 days, I don't know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we know that by the time that Mr. Susa and Mr. Bogunovic met with the JNA colonel on the 30th of December, he was clearly deputy prime minister at that point because that's how he was introduced and referred to. You need to say yes or no. You can't just nod your head. It doesn't make it into the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's not that I was nodding by way of a response. I was nodding to myself. And one can see it not only from this, i.e. Bogunovic's appearance in Ilok, but I think it was also published in the Official Gazette, both when he became minister of police and deputy prime minister, so it's not only that. There are several sources from which one can see when this took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My point here, Mr. Hadzic, is Mr. Bogunovic is decommissioned as minister of the interior because, as you said, he wasn't professional. He was just not professional enough. He seemed ill-equipped to handle Ministry of Interior. So what you then did is to promote him and put him with Susa in charge of housing. Again, it seems a decision calculated to -- well, why did you do that? Why did you promote him, put him in charge of housing, when it's clear to you he's not professional and he couldn't handle the job that he'd already had?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Bogunovic was a layperson for the police, but Boro Bogunovic was a man who was capable of doing other things. He worked in a big company in Vukovar before the war and he was a capable person. When I said that he was not a professional, I meant that he was not a professional for the police. He did not have a good co-operation with the police from Serbia, and Badza was their boss. Badza was the boss of the entire police force in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and he did not want to cooperate with him. And Boro was capable of doing other jobs too, and that is why he got promoted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Hadzic please slow down and repeat the rest of his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you get that message, Mr. Hadzic? They're asking if you could slow down and repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Badza had under his control the entire police. That includes the territory of Slavonia and Baranja. And he did not want -- I mean, he did not find a common tongue with Boro Bogunovic and Boro was not a professional for the police. But Boro was a man who could have done this work of a different kind. Now, Boro, when he was appointed minister of police, that was not just my decision. At the time when it's government was formed, I was not some kind of a big boss that I could have decided you'd be that. I wasn't above Boro. This was a joint decision of ours that Boro would be minister of the police. This was just in a formal sense because the police did not even exist at the time and the assembly appointed Boro deputy prime minister at my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tab 1512, please, P3184.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I just want to look at numbers for a couple of more minutes. This is a March 10th of 1992 report coming from Tovarnik village, from the JNA commander there, regarding the national structure and number of inhabitants in the zone of the 3rd Motorised Brigade. And if we go then to the next page, we see another one of these charts regarding ethnic composition pre- and post-conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the English there, before "b/d," you'll see in the footnote "b/d" means "combat operation." So these are numbers before and after combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just want to look at some of these, Mr. Hadzic, not all of them. You tell me if you disagree with -- if you have any strong disagreement with the data that's presented in this. Tovarnik pre-conflict, pre-combat activities about 2100 Croats, 262 Croats after combat activities. Whereas at the same time we have 852 Serbs who lived there who after the conflict are now joined by 950 people who had come in, Serbs who came in to settle. Ilaca had 15 Serbs pre-conflict and 550 after. Again, Serb settlers. So skipping ahead to page 5 of the English, population by national structure in the area of responsibility of the Ilok Town Command, 8500 Croats before, 1826 after. The number of Serbs here remains relatively -- excuse me. If we see before combat operations 1167 Serbs. After combat operations, the number of Serbs who had lived there before remains relatively the same but now we see inhabited, which I'm suggesting is settlers, an additional 4314 Serbs who have arrived. So would you agree with me, Mr. Hadzic, that what is happening - and I'm not going to go through all of this, it continues on, Ilok, Sarengrad, Mohovo, Bapska - but we don't really have any strong disagreement, do we, that as of March 10th, 1992, there had been a profound change in the ethnic composition of this Western Srem region that's referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this report shows that they're using the concept of military administration in the area of responsibility. That is to say that everything that happened, happened under the command of and in the organisation of the JNA. However, I as a witness do not know anything about this because I did not take part in any of this and I did not have this information. But speaking as a private person, I know that people came from Western Slavonia, Serbs, and the Croats left with their army. That I know, sort of. But it's not that I took part in any of this and that I can testify about any of that. I don't -- I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just setting aside the issue of responsibility and even setting aside the issue of why Croats left, my question is: Based upon whether it's your capacity as president of the RSK, which you were at this time, or as a private citizen, I take it you don't take strong -- you don't have strong disagreement with the notion that there was profound demographic change that had occurred in Western Srem as of this time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could agree. I know the Croats left and the Serbs from Western Slavonia came. That's all I know, and I think that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1514, P2754.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is from roughly the same period, 16 March 1992, a report to the 1st Military District Command, "Weekly report of the organ for civil affairs." Turning to page 2, first of all, I want to see -- apologies. The top of page 2, talking about replacing personal documents, issuing them with documents certified by the SBWS government. And then: "In order to resolve this problem, the organ for civil affairs has addressed the issue to the SO government, municipal authorities. To facilitate solution to this problem in accordance with your abilities, exercise influence on the government of Serbia and through them on the Serbian district government. The authorities of the government of SO SBWS are not sufficiently present on the ground and are inefficient at resolving important problems." Why didn't you take measures to -- because you know from your exchange with Mr. Belic going back to December that there was inadequate and insufficient co-ordination and involvement between your government and the JNA military authorities, why didn't you do any more to fix that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several reasons. The first reason is that we did not deal with the problem of settlement and resettlement at all. It was not our priority and the government did not get involved in this at all. Second, we were taken by surprise by these events, as you can see from Belic's letter, and we were accused that we were doing nothing, which is completely contrary to the relevant count in the indictment. And, third, there was a military rule there. You can see from the date, 16 March, that the military rule was still there and they were still dealing with these issues, and did not allow us to deal with them. So this commission headed by Bogunovic and Susa, in Ilok, tried to do something, but they couldn't because it was still administered by military rule. And when we raised the issue of finances, that's when there was a real problem. They didn't even want to discuss it, because they took everything in their own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You just said "that we did not deal with the problem of settlement and resettlement at all." In fact, Mr. Hadzic, that's not true. You were the lead negotiator in the international negotiations taking place about the Vance Plan, and the Vance Plan and your involvement in it was all about settlement and resettlement. How can you claim that you didn't have any involvement or participation or deal with the problem of settlement and resettlement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you and explain this easily. First of all, there are my arguments and the arguments of the opposing side who is accusing me of something. In Milan Ilic's previous letter, the theory was that Milan Ilic wanted to settle Serbs in that area. Now it is obvious to me from this that it was the JNA that wanted to settle the Serbs. And I was dealing with the Vance Plan, and I accepted the Vance Plan, according to which the refugees were supposed to return when the conditions are met. On the 16th of March, the date here, there was no talk about this. It's quite obvious from this that the JNA had a different plan that the government and I knew nothing about. At the time we are discussing, my government was already disbanded. It didn't exist. So when I said that we didn't deal with it, I meant the government of which I was prime minister. It was obvious that our priority was not to move Croats out and move Serbs in. Instead, Belic's invitation to join him in Ilok 16 caught us by surprise. And after February, that government no longer existed. The problem of the Vance Plan is something you are right about, but in a wrong way. The Vance Plan requested the return of refugees, all refugees, once it became possible. And even when refugees sometimes wanted to return, even by force, UNPROFOR was against them returning at that time, because they said that the conditions for that had not been created, and that their return would cause conflict and new problems on the ground, as the wounds were still fresh and the people who had until the day before waged war could not suddenly live in peace together until the conditions for that were created. The conditions were created a couple of years later. It's obvious that this JNA officer was advocated something that I did not agree with. I stand by my position as I stood by it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next paragraph in this document says that: "With the SO government's permission, the local authorities are continuing to move out the Croatian population. On 15 March 1992 approximately 100 inhabitants were removed from Boksic village. According to our information, the removal is carried out pursuant to compiled lists and they are mainly persons who are involved in any way in the Croatian Defence Forces or are still collaborating with them on a voluntary basis." Now, the fact is that even though you'd moved on to be president of the republic, the SBWS government and the people you left behind there were continuing to employ this policy of removing Croats in order to maintain the newly achieved Serbian demographic majorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You said they continued that policy. They couldn't continue that policy because the SBWS government did not have such a policy. You don't need to be a rocket scientist to understand who is writing this and how they are writing. It was happening in the area of responsibility of the JNA. Nobody from the government could even come there without JNA permission. It was completely controlled by the JNA. I don't know for whom these lies are intended, whether this officer is lying to himself, as he can't lie to me, or whether - why he is writing this at all. Who could come to the area of responsibility of the JNA at the time? They, the JNA, didn't let us leave our own villages without a special permit. There was this problem too. Who could take 100 people in the plain sight of a brigade - of a JNA brigade with 50 tanks and all the colonels whom we couldn't even approach? I'm really surprised that anybody could believe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So now this is Novica Gusic, Mr. Hadzic. Is he also lying when he says that this was done with the SO government's permission? Is this another JNA officer who is just lying about what's happening in his own area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he is lying. He is lying shamelessly. What government permission? Which government? What could the government order to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so then you're telling us, Mr. Hadzic, that all of these -- this gentleman's a colonel and the JNA assistant commander for civil affairs, he is lying to his superiors in the 1st Military District Command about the removal of 100 Croat inhabitants from Boksic village. That's -- that's your view? This is an absolute false report.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said he is saying half the truth and half lies. In the first half, he is telling the truth, that it is under their administration, military rule, under their control and that this was done. Now, in order to keep it on record, he is lying that somebody else had done it, not them. So he's telling about 60 per cent of truth and 40 per cent of lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So all of the expulsions and the displacements of the non-Serbs from Western Srem, in your view, were carried out exclusively by the JNA. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the JNA area of responsibility, who could come, at all? The government that we are talking about, that remained after me, their main problem was still how to distribute...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started, but you didn't let me finish. For our government, it was a big problem how to distribute personal incomes. They didn't have a single bus, they didn't even have a car. How could the government transport 100 people when they didn't have cars for themselves? I'm quite sure that nobody from the government could come to Boksic even if they wanted to. For a number of reasons. First of all, because the army was there and, second of all, because the government had 7 neither cars nor petrol to come there. So how could the government have given a permission, so that Gusic could see it and consequently write something like this? It is written in such an obviously biased and false manner.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Hadzic please stop speaking so fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you are speaking way too fast. Please keep that in mind when giving answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I just noted one error either in -- in transcript or in translation. It is in line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No wonder, Mr. Zivanovic, with the speech -- with the -- with the velocity with which Mr. Hadzic is talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. It is page 54, line 8. It is -- it states: "How could we transport 100 people ..." Because he -- as far as I heard, he said: "How could they transport 100 people when they didn't have cars for themselves?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I was talking about that government in which I was no longer a member. I'm sorry I speeded up because when the Prosecutor interrupted me, I speeded up because I was afraid he might interrupt me again. But I won't do it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it your view, Mr. Hadzic, that the JNA is exclusively responsible for expulsions and displacement of non-Serbs also in the Dalj municipality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a different matter. I don't know how the expulsions were enforced in the Dalj municipality. If you can show me some evidence, some papers about the organisation of that, but that could not be done without the permission of the JNA. Maybe some fools, maybe some self-appointed people did that. But without the approval of the JNA that could not be done. The JNA controlled the entire territory. Not a single bicycle could pass by that check-point unseen, let alone a whole bus. I cannot talk about any other details. But nothing could happen there without the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was the JNA exclusively responsible for the displacements, the expulsions of non-Serbs from the Baranja region, Beli Manastir, in your view?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the entire territory of Baranja was controlled by the JNA, but I was not so familiar with the Baranja area and I have no particular information. But I'm again sure that it couldn't be done without the JNA because the entire border, both facing Serbia and facing Croatia, was controlled by the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serb -- Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is that displacement and expulsion of non-Serbs was vital to you and your government and its ability to hold on to the SBWS region in all of these places because there had not been a Serbian majority there before. Your view was that the expulsion was necessary and needed to be maintained.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not a fact. Our position was completely contrary. I'll hope I'll make myself clear enough for the Trial Chamber to understand. During combat operations and after their completion, large numbers of Croatian people withdrew together with their army and a smaller number of them remained, those who wished to stay. For me, and the government I represented, they were not a problem. On the contrary. It was in our interest for them to stay there because we wanted to remain a part of Yugoslavia. And as an ethnically pure territory it would not be good. So it was constantly a problem for us that I faced very frequently as the President of the Republic, the problem was in Knin. I was - although I had no power against these expulsions. And according to the information I now have, some Croats left because they were expelled but some left voluntarily, in order to be reunited with their families. Because our authorities were not giving them permits to leave. It was in our interest that they stay, but they made do in various ways, they managed, and it was only when UNPROFOR came to the area that many of them left, with the help of UNPROFOR. It was not my personal policy that Croats should leave Slavonia and Baranja, because as I have just said, we did not expect some elections at which the balance would be tipped, so that there would be a Croatian majority in certain areas, which would then be a problem. No, that was not our thinking. We wanted to stay within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have tab 1218, please, P41.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a UN cable to Mr. Goulding from Mr. Nambiar on 9th of July, 1992, regarding their meeting with you, Mr. Dzakula, and your foreign minister Mr. Vejzovic. And I want to direct your attention to paragraph 10 because what you just said, Mr. Hadzic, was a lie. This business about wanting the Croats to stay. This is how it really was and we see it in paragraph 10: "On the question of refugees, Hadzic said that they were prepared to accept all non-Serbs who were willing to return to the UNPAs, but at the same time it must be realised that even if all non-Serbs were to return, the Serbs would still remain in the majority." And that was absolutely your position as president of the RSK, as president of the republic, that in those areas which you had finally achieved Serbian control demographically you were going to keep it that way and make sure that not enough Croats came back to be able to take the majority again as it had been before the conflict. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I don't want to use any harsher word. There is no need for conflation here, and I'll speak slowly now so that the interpreters can follow. A moment ago we discussed Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Now we moved on to the Republic of Serbian Krajina. What we saw in this paragraph 10, I think, I don't have it anymore, this conversation, two unconnected conclusions were conflated. It was in my interest and the interest of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to remain a multi-ethnic community and for the Vance Plan to be implemented as planned and as much as possible. It's not because we wanted to be still a majority. In the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in the SAO Krajina, even before the conflict, there were 90 per cent Serbs. Even if all Croats had returned, they wouldn't have had any problems. The Serbs would still have remained the majority, but that's not important for our discussion at all. It just proves that we didn't mind the Croats coming back. Why would it be a problem if someone wanted to return and live in their own home? Knin was 90 per cent Serb. I'm not saying that is - that is either good or bad, or that these 10 per cent of Croats would have to disappear. But that is a fact. And I don't see why you tell me I'm lying when I say that I never minded Croats who wanted to remain with us in Yugoslavia, or any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it time for the break, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, before the break, we were looking at P41 which was the UN cable talking about this statement of yours that you were "prepared to accept all non-Serbs who were willing to return to the UNPAs," plural, "but at the same time it must be realised that even if all non-Serbs were to return, the Serbs would still remain in the majority." I'm going to put it to you, Mr. Hadzic, that you're talking about this issue of majority, that is, the demographic aspect, because you knew that that was the key to your government's ability to hold on to the SBWS. You had to preserve the status quo that had been achieved during the war which was the ethnic cleansing and expulsion of non-Serbs. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The interpretation I got was SBWS. Did you perhaps misspeak? Because this is not about Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It's about the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Could you just give me the whole thing back in Serbian so I can see it once again and then I would like to explain that Serbs would still be in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could show Mr. Hadzic paragraph 10 in the B/C/S. I think we don't have that in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand the context. I said it only as a confirmation, that this accusation that we didn't want Croats to come back, as allegedly the Serbs would not then be in the majority, I said that this accusation doesn't hold water because in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the Serbs would still be in the majority even if all the Croats returned. So this accusation that we were afraid of it, that we didn't want it, is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, actually, this paragraph talks about the UN Protected Areas in the plural, and whether we talked about the UNPAs or whether we talk about the RSK, we're still talking about the area of the SBWS. True? The SBWS was one of the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but for me that was the Republic of Serbian Krajina as a whole and we didn't discuss separately that refugees could return to one area and not to another area. When we discussed the return of refugees, we discussed their return to the whole territory, and that meant to the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We never discussed -- I never discussed separate parts of that region, and I don't remember that anybody ever specifically mentioned one area as different from the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just in the preceding paragraph 9 here, you're being asked about the matter of the expulsions in Tovarnik. So we know that despite what you're claiming now, certainly the discussion with these gentlemen from the UN included the SBWS; right? Tovarnik being in Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just explained it a moment ago. I discussed the entire territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, including everything, and including Tovarnik, which was in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And could you please show me para 9 again so I can see what's written about Tovarnik. Yes, I remember that question. I remember it was put to me when I came here, and I saw that some of these people were prosecuted, that some of them had been caught and some of them hadn't. But most of the perpetrators of that crime were caught and put on trial, specifically for Tovarnik. It was not strictly my job, but I happen to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll talk about that probably tomorrow. On the 14th of July, Mr. Hadzic, this year on your direct testimony you were asked about this issue of what we call special status, and your counsel referred you or said as a question, he said: "You also said the most acceptable option is the one involving special status. Were those your words?" And your answer was -- this is page 9719 of the transcript. You said: "Yes, those were my words. We in Slavonia, Baranja, were prepared to discuss a special status but certain preconditions had to be met and it couldn't happen overnight." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I think it had to do with my conversation with Mr. Henry Wijnaendts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right, and also Ambassador Ahrens who testified earlier in this trial. And in the context of Messrs Wijnaendts and Ahrens, then, when we talk about special status, can we agree, Mr. Hadzic, that that involves some degree of autonomy or special status for Serbs who were in these areas of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not discussed in detail but the very word "special status" indicates that it was some sort of special status, but I don't remember the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But you knew that certainly in your dealings with the international community, Wijnaendts, Ahrens, others, there wasn't going to be any special status for Serbs in Western Slavonia -- excuse me, in SBWS because they'd never had majority population in that area. Special status was only going to apply to Serb-majority areas such as the Knin Krajina. Isn't that how it was explained to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would Wijnaendts then inform me and not Babic who didn't want to discuss it? Wherever Serbs were in Croatia, they were supposed to have some sort of special status with special rights, regardless of the territory. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab number 44, which is 65 ter 1D02579.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is a report or a note dated 23 July 1992 and it's setting out what was said at a meeting two days earlier on the 21st of July, 1992, in which you met with Lord Carrington and others. Also present was your foreign minister, Mr. Vejzovic, Defence Minister Stojan Spanovic. Mr. Ahrens was there as well. And the 21st of July being, well, the same month that you had met with Messrs. Goulding and Nambiar in the document we were just looking at a minute ago. It's about 12 days later. On page -- bottom of page 2 of the English, it says: "Ambassador Ahrens did not agree to stray from the task ..." That's where the paragraph begins. And I don't have the B/C/S reference for you, unfortunately. I believe it would be page 2 of the B/C/S as well. It begins: "Ambassador Ahrens did not agree to stray from the task ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it goes on to say: "Ambassador Ahrens responded to this remark by saying that the Republic of Serbian Krajina had two serious issues: Firstly, the RSK is part of Croatia and is not completely independent, and secondly, the basis for decision will be the census of 1981 or 1991, according to which the Serbs have a majority in 11 municipalities and a relative majority in Pakrac and Petrinja, but in Beli Manastir, the Serbs account for only 26 per cent. After the return of refugees to the 11 municipalities, the Serbian majority will be restored, and that will be the basis for making a decision, but the other municipalities will not be part of the autonomous community (read: RSK)." Now, Mr. Hadzic, the message that's being delivered to you here - and I'd suggest that, according to his evidence, Ambassador Ahrens delivered this message to you more than once - the 11 municipalities here are going to be a reference to the Serbian Krajina. Whereas, as referred to here, Beli Manastir, where there was only 26 per cent Serb, Beli Manastir is never going to be a part of any sort of autonomous community. It's never going to enjoy any sort of special status. Isn't that what they were telling you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all able to hear the testimony of Mr. Ahrens. He said what he had to say about my conduct and the conduct of all the others who were there. I have nothing to add to that. This was our thinking at the time. Now, it says here that if it were to be the main principle, only the 1981 and 1991 censuses would be used, and in that case there was no point in expelling anyone. That's why I was not in favour of expelling people. And Mr. Ahrens could tell you first-hand what I was thinking about the whole issue. And it confirms what I'm saying now, that I was prepared to talk and to negotiate and work for a peaceful and stable solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But what Mr. Ahrens was telling you at the time was that you were never going to be able to hold on to the SBWS as some sort of autonomous region or territory because it had never been a region in which Serbs formed a majority of the population; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what is written here. I don't remember that exactly, but that turned out to be true. That is ultimately what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so you knew that your only chance of holding on to SBWS as an autonomous region was to preserve the newly achieved ethnic composition in which you did now have a Serbian majority achieved through expulsion. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the truth. It is actually the direct opposite of what you've been showing us just now. What we were told was that irrespective of the momentary situation, it is 1981 and 1991 that are going to be taken into account and that the current state of affairs really had no effect and that it really -- that there was no point. It's only the census of 1981 and 1991 that would be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender that exhibit, 1D02579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, on the 10th of July, this summer, last month, on your direct examination you were asked a few questions about Mr. Stevo Bogic and I'd like to follow up on that. At page 9689 of the transcript, you -- actually what was happening at the time, my learned friend, Mr. Zivanovic, was taking you through the Law on Ministries, I believe it was, in which all of the people who had been appointed ministers of the SBWS government were listed there. Do you remember that? And he was asking you about where everyone had come from.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you were asked about Mr. Bogic and you said: "He was from Borovo Selo. He came as part of the package together with Jovic and Devetak." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, he was a minister without a portfolio. I think I asked you about this earlier. You'd indicated previously, I think in your suspect interview, that he didn't have an education or was not well educated and so he could not be given a portfolio.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was not specifically professional for a particular ministry or department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you went on to describe his duties in which he was responsible -- well, I'll just read your words at 9690: "He assumed a responsibility to set up a security service around the government building. That meant around-the-clock security detail in three shifts." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I said that, and I remember that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honours - I don't think we need to look at it - the reference was to L -- Exhibit L1, page 24 of the English, which is the decision appointing Mr. Bogic as well as the other ministers of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Bogic's profession or his employment prior to the time he became a minister without a portfolio?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was an agricultural technician by training.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you meet him in Borovo Selo around the events of the -- the time of the incident there in May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not meet with him. I think I didn't even know him at the time. I mean, I didn't talk to him. I hadn't talked to him. Maybe I saw him before, but it's not that we were friends or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My -- my question, and let me put it to you this way. When did you first become acquainted with Mr. Bogic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in the summer of 1991. I think. I knew him then by name and surname. Perhaps I saw him at a meeting before that, but I didn't know who he was. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then could you just briefly describe, then, how your relationship with him developed such that then he was entrusted with the duty of establishing and organising this security detail for the government buildings.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I stated that up until now, but when I said that he was in charge of security for the government, it's not that I personally gave him that duty. I didn't even know him then. It was the government decision and he became minister at the proposal of the local commune of Borovo Selo, as I've already said, in that package, like Devetak. I didn't even know Devetak. I just knew Dr. Jovic. I mean, I knew Dr. Jovic better.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bogic have a background or training in security, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Moving forward, then, into 1992 and beyond, he also was a minister in the government of the RSK; correct? Excuse me, he was deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was deputy prime minister of the RSK and he was elected at this assembly in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During that period, did Mr. Bogic also play a role linked to security?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during the assembly? While the assembly was held?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps, yes. But just in general terms, during the RSK period, beginning in early 1992, did he play a role in respect of security for the assembly, for members of government, for transporting individuals, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, that is to say, in 1991, from time to time he would help and organise that, but I don't have any information about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 97, Exhibit 1D03600.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is from Danas, 16 July 1991. Title is: "No talks with the Croats." This is in Borovo. And there is a part of this that attributes some statements to Mr. Bogic and then another part that attributes statements to you. And in the first paragraph here we see, it says: "These ideas shattered against the statement of Stevo Bogic who admits that the Croatian authorities had issued several wanted notices against him and they were just waiting for Serbia to recognise as its own territory Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem. There will be no talks with the Croats. There are too many insults, too many victims fell, so living together is no longer possible." What --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find that in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the original doesn't match to -- doesn't correspond to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll move ahead then. We'll come back to it, Mr. President. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, Mr. President, is at tab 1047. It's a video-clip. Exhibit P241. We have this as the 29th of July, 1991. And we -- the interpreters should have it, the transcript, and we'll wait for them to tell us if they've got it at hand before we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the 65 ter or the V number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 4895.1. Can we start?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes. Interpreter's note: We've got it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Branko Kostic visited Borovo Selo today. Talking to the citizens, Kostic stated, among other things, that those defending their homes could not be referred to as bandits or terrorists. He criticised the federal government for, as he maintained, insufficient support ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we've stopped the video there, and I'm going to ask you if you can identify a couple of the people -- a few of the people we see in the frame. First of all, to the right of the screen, our right-hand side, the gentleman in the light-coloured suit, who's that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Branko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think he was vice-president of the Presidency of the SFRY and acting president or something like that; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall this occasion of his visit to Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he came. I don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you accept if I suggested that this is on the 29th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would accept that, yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then seated next to Mr. Kostic we see that's you signing something. And then I want to move over -- moving to the left of the screen, there's a gentleman standing with a light-coloured shirt that's open at the collar. Can you identify him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is Stevo Bogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to show you a few more of these videos, Mr. Hadzic, because just to suggest to you, it appears to me - and you can correct me if I'm wrong - given his proximity, is he standing close to you because is he providing some level of security? Is this related to his function on the security side or is he there for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just happened to be there. It is not security. He personally was not capable of carrying out security-related work. He had a physical handicap. He had a problem with his leg. I mean, I don't want to offend him, but it would have been ridiculous if I were to say that he personally could have provided security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next one is tab 1022, Exhibit P3128, which would be 65 ter 4831.1. When the interpreters have that, we'll start.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We've found it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "'This moment was worth living for.' These were the words that Ilija Koncarevic, the president of the Great National Assembly of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, used to address the deputies, announcing the decision that Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, together with the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, constitute a new federal unit of the Serbian people. And the Assembly of the SAO Krajina proclaimed Krajina a republic at today's session in Knin, enacted its constitution, and elected Dr. Milan Babic as its first president by unanimous vote. "The Great National Assembly of the Serbian region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem adopted the new constitution, by which it proclaimed the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The new state ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is Beli Manastir in December of 1991, proclamation of the RSK? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, yes. Yes. Yes. I didn't understand that that was the question. Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then we see you seated right in the middle of the screen there in the green uniform; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who is the gentleman seated next to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the minister of foreign affairs in that government of ours, Professor Dr. Caslav Ocic. He is a member of the Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can run the video a bit more if it will assist, but before we do that, could I just suggest to you that seated behind you in the green uniform is again Mr. Bogic at this -- at this -- at this assembly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation I received said "again." That would have meant that he had been sitting behind me before this, or maybe this is just a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. Is that Mr. Bogic who is seated behind you that we see on the screen, the gentleman in the green -- what appears to be a green uniform?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Vitomir Devetak is sitting behind me and it is behind Caslav Ocic that he is sitting. And behind me on this side, like Bogic is on the other side, is Milan Milanovic and he is to Devetak's left and Bogic is on his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So just for the record, in the row of people behind you then, starting at the right-hand side of the screen, that's Mr. Milan Milanovic, Mr. Vitomir Devetak, Mr. Stevo Bogic, and then who is the fourth gentleman, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is some guest from Novi Sad. I don't know him. He's not from the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, why were you and these two members of your -- well, who had been members of your SBWS government, Mr. Milanovic and Mr. Bogic, wearing uniforms? Why are you still wearing uniforms at this time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this was December 1991. UNPROFOR hadn't come yet. There was still a war going on, and I've already explained this, why I wore a uniform and why I wasn't wearing civilian clothes. But maybe I should explain it again if it is of interest. I know why I wore a uniform. I don't know why Bogic wore a uniform and I'm not sure that what he is wearing is a uniform. I really don't know anything about him. But I am wearing the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next document, I don't know that we need to call it up, I'll just say it for the record, Mr. Hadzic. If you want to take a look at it, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, let's -- let's -- let's go there. This would be tab 424, which is Exhibit L6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what we're looking at here, Mr. Hadzic, is item number 140. This is the Official Gazette of the RSK, decision on the election of the prime minister and government ministers. And here we see Mr. Bogic, number 4, as having been elected minister of the government. Do you know what his function was in this capacity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know was that he was elected deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What did he bring to the government that justified that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see before whom you think this should be justified. It was the Assembly that elected him then. The government was still not – it was formed only on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. But you must -- as president of the republic, you must know what it was that he was expected to do; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not. This was the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina that was proposed and appointed and confirmed by the assembly. Actually, it was proposed by Zdravko Zecevic, the prime minister. I didn't know half of these people who were in the government, and it was Zecevic who compiled this personnel list of this. I only proposed Zecevic, I mean, and it was the assembly that elected him and them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the same Zdravko Zecevic that I asked you about earlier in your testimony before the summer recess. He's the gentleman at the SFRY Presidency talking about how the Croats can't come back to Benkovac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just know one Zdravko Zecevic and that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so he also then proposed Mr. Bogic and the others to be members of his government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the procedure was. The prime minister proposes his cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I mean, as time went on, you became friends with Mr. Bogic, though; right? It's not just that you were president and he was a deputy prime minister. You had a friendly relationship with Mr. Bogic that developed over time. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time not yet. I became friends later when I lived from time to time in Borovo Selo, and that's where he was from. I didn't particularly socialise with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's your evidence that you really don't know what his function was as -- let me ask you this: In general, did you know what was the role or the function of a deputy prime minister in the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that I did not know what his function was. I said that he was deputy prime minister. He attended regular meetings of the government, but he did not report to me. Zdravko Zecevic didn't report to me either. He probably carried out some work in which he was guided by the prime minister. That is only something that I can assume but I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know if he represented the RSK government in meetings of local officials throughout the republic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I assume that that could have been the case. I didn't know at that time and nobody reported to me about that, but he probably did something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as a deputy prime minister of the RSK government, then, I expect that his -- he would be obligated professionally to carry out the policy of the RSK government as one of its representatives.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be logical. But it was an issue for the government, and the government was chosen by the assembly. It was a body parallel to the president of the republic. Our competences did not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1049, which is P2199. This is a video. 65 ter 4896.2. And we'll wait for the interpreters to say when they're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Serbs in Krajina, or at least some of them, have decided to welcome the Blue Helmets well prepared and trained. This is no time for quarrel but for unity, harmony, and coexistence of the Serbian people in one state, was one of the messages heard today at a meeting in the 17th August training centre of the Krajina SUP located in Golubic near Knin. The meeting was held to mark the beginning of the training of the first class of Krajina MUP policemen and was attended by many dignitaries, including members of the rump Yugoslavia Presidency Jugoslav Kostic and Sejdo Bajramovic, also Goran Hadzic and Mile Paspalj, and the representatives of the Yugoslav army headed by the commander of the Knin Corps Major-General Ratko Mladic, as well as the representatives of the SUP of Serbia. After the anthems 'Hej, Sloveni' and 'Boze pravde' were played and after the troop review, Milan Martic addressed the policemen."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We stopped the video at this point, Mr. Hadzic, again just we see you standing there -- well, first of all, do you remember what this event is? We've seen this video a few times.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I have a brain freeze. I remember we were there, and I remember watching this video but I can't remember. My concentration has dropped. I would be grateful if you could remind me a little. But I know we have already discussed it. It was some sort of celebration or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is what we would call the rally or the ceremony that was held at Golubic in spring of 1992. Does that sound correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it was in Golubic. It was in 1992, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the gentleman standing next to you, who's that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Zdravko Zecevic, the late.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then standing next to him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is Deputy Prime Minister Stevo Bogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, again, I had intended to suggest or to ask whether his proximity to you again is linked to his function in some security capacity, but based on what you've said, I guess that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Behind my back you see the head of Ljubomir Mudrinic, between me and Zdravko Zecevic. That's my security. And my second escort, Milenko Japundzic, must be standing next to him but we can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And those are the two gentlemen who I believe you've testified were your closest security people really since the beginning when you became president of the SBWS government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were my only escorts throughout 1991. Stevo Bogic is not standing there as my security man. He is here as a guest, in terms of protocol, because we are lined up according to hierarchy – the President of the Republic, the Prime Minister and he as the Deputy Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, by -- well, you indicated that at some point, you -- because you were both living in Borovo Selo, you and Mr. Bogic then formed some sort of a relationship of a friendship. When did that start?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the elections in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I occasionally stayed at Borovo Selo. That was in 1994. And then I used to see him more often. But we never had a problem with each other. We were on good terms even before but we were not friends. We didn't sit around in bars together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next one is tab 979, Exhibit P3124, 65 ter 4795.5. And again we'll wait for the interpreters to tell us when they're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can't see the 65 ter number on the screen yet. Could you remind us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "So, on 19 February 1995, there was a wedding of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, commander of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and president of the Serbian Unity, and Svetlana Ceca Velickovic, the most popular singer of Serbia and Yugoslavia. The arrival from -- in Zitoradja is as planned. It's still raining a bit, but nobody seems to mind. I will also tell you who the guests of the wedding party are: The host ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, we probably don't need all of this, Mr. President. I'm just going to ask if my colleague Mr. Laugel can move us ahead to about the one-minute mark of the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... Janko Raznjatovic, uncle; vojvoda, or duke, Vuk Vukovic; ensign - Zeljko Raznjatovic's eldest son Mihajlo; best man ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just we're seeing now this image, the question is: You attended Zeljko Raznjatovic's wedding; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: February 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was 1995. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is that Mr. Bogic who is seated next to you on your left here in this image we're seeing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then as I understand it, at some point around this time, maybe earlier, you actually -- I don't know how to put it the most correctly, but you're perhaps the godfather of his daughter. He asked you to be the godfather of his daughter at her baptism. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a Serbian custom and it's a sin to refuse when you're invited to be the godfather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, whose daughter is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise. The daughter of Stevo Bogic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Hadzic? We're talking about the daughter of Mr. Bogic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 414, P00201.140. It's a document, not a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While this is coming up, Mr. Hadzic, by way of introduction I think we're going to move to an aspect of this topic which perhaps we will disagree about more than we have so far on Mr. Bogic. My understanding from your evidence is that you deny that there was some entity or group called the Serbian National Security, what we call in English SNB. Is that your evidence: It didn't exist?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my evidence. It didn't exist, except in colloquial terms. About those people who were standing guard around the government, some were saying in jest that they were guarding the “think-tank” of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, that they were guarding the Serbian nation in a way. The Serbian National Security was more of a pejorative term, because that didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're not getting e-court. We don't see the document on our screen in e-court. I don't know if anyone else is having a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We have the same problem, indeed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Someone is looking into it, Mr. Stringer. Can we proceed or do we wait?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think for the document we need to -- to -- we need to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could see if I could skip ahead of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've seen this before, Mr. Hadzic. I know for sure you saw it your suspect interview because you were asked about it. This is dated the 10th of February, 1992. Upper left-hand corner, it says: "Serbian National Security, Erdut." And it appears over -- well, can you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it's written "Stevo Bogic." I don't know exactly what his signature looks like, but I suppose this could be it. I'm not sure, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what's happening here is that Mr. Bogic -- well, looking at the original, and we can blow it up, if necessary, do you have any reason to doubt the -- the seal that appears next to his name there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This stamp is the stamp of one of the ministries or of the government, but it's not the stamp of the Serbian National Security because it didn't exist, so it certainly isn't that stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking if it's a stamp of the Serbian National Security. I think you've answered my question. Your evidence is that this does appear to be a stamp of one of the ministries of the government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. It could be, but I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on the translation, what we have is that it's the stamp of the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, Vukovar. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's written. But I don't remember that stamp. It must have been made at some ministry. It was not the stamp of my office, or the office of the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now we just got that you said: "It was not the stamp of my office, the office of the prime minister." But now this is February 1992. So at that point, your office is the office of the president; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a special stamp. The only stamp I had was the stamp of the secretary of the government, but this is not it. I didn't have any special office until I became president of the republic and that was only after the 26th of February. This is before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There's some handwriting on the -- well, first of all, what's happening here is that Mr. Bogic is sending in this specification of requirements stating that they need funds amounting to 260.000 dinars for one month and this is based on the work of the Serbian National Security Service. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So at least as of February 1992, Mr. Bogic thinks there is something called Serbian National Security; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it might appear so from this. You need to ask Bogic. I didn't have that information, and it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then there's handwriting that can you see on this document. And the handwriting on the left-hand side says: "It was agreed that Bogdan should call, in other words, that it should not go into procedure until the other ministries are also resolved." That's 19th February, 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then at the bottom of the right hand -- in the bottom right-hand corner it says: "At the recommendation of President Hadzic, approved by," and we have the signature of Mr. Vojnovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's Bogdan Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it's Bogdan Vojnovic. Because there was only another Vojnovic, Milos, but this is a B.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you remind us what was Mr. Bogdan Vojnovic's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the minister of finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You don't doubt that that's his signature on the document, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no because I've never seen his signature. I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But you don't have any reason to doubt what is indicated in this document, though, do you, in terms of his approving the funds going, as requested, to Mr. Bogic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to either doubt it or not doubt it. I can only say it was not at my recommendation. I don't know about the rest, and I don't know what the purpose of this was. The only thing I remember is that in February some money was supposed to come in to finance the work of the government, and this was just an attempt to launder it or to justify it. I can only assume that. Because I learned that now, from the investigators, I didn't even know about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, do you think that Mr. Bogic is involved in trying to embezzle money from the government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't go as far as to say that, but I think he wanted to pay salaries to the people who were guarding the government. That's my guess. Because from what I know, they had worked for an entire year without pay. When I say the whole year, I mean those couple of months in 1991, not the whole year, because they had perhaps only been working in October, November and December.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 432, Exhibit P1834.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you were asked to comment on this document during your direct examination. This was on the 16th of July, page 9869 to 70. And at 9869 you said that: "As for the Serbian National Security, I've already explained it didn't exist. It was just misinformation spread among the people." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we turn to page 5 of the English, which is -- I believe it's also page 5 of the B/C/S, Mr. Hadzic, I'm looking at the paragraph that begins with the words: "Namely, at the time of disrupted values and general distrust, aware of their advantage ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "... obvious distrust of the SJB," which I believe is the public security station, "and the SDB," which is the security service, I believe "certain individuals have established security services like: The Serbian National Security and the security services in the TO Staffs, Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's unit, is also used for this purpose." And then skipping down a paragraph, it again refers to Serbian National Security. "We're pointing here to the illegal opening of the positions in the SJB by the Serbian National Security ..." Following paragraph refers to the members of the Serbian National Security. And then the next paragraph after that, it says: "The culmination of dissatisfaction was caused by the information that the work of the Assembly of Krajina on 25 February 1992 was ensured by the Serbian National Security and the unit of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility, Mr. Hadzic, that even if you didn't know it was calling itself this, there was a group of people linked to Mr. Bogic who did call themselves Serbian National Security, SNB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't call themselves like that. It was a group that was in charge of the security for the building. And the residents of Borovo Selo, because most of them were from Borovo Selo, called them different names, mockingly, pejoratively, and one of those names that became the most commonly used one was the National Security, Serbian National Security, but they were saying that they were guarding the think-tank, the conglomeration of the most precious brains we had. In short, those were the jokes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to make sure I understand you clearly on this. Some people out there were referring to these security people as Serbian National Security? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was in jest because they were up to ten people, eight, nine or ten. They were based in Erdut and they provided non-stop security for the government while their neighbours had to take up arms and go to war. So these people obviously resented them, were jealous of them, and called them different names, including derogatory ones. Those people had to go to war whereas, in their opinion, this group remained in the rear. They guarded the premises of the government around the clock, working in three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then it's indicated here, did they also become involved in providing security at the Krajina Assembly on the 25th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already given evidence on this issue. It's possible they brought some ministers. There could have been no more than three or four of them, because at least as many of them must have remained in Erdut. And they were standing at the door because they knew these people, so they knew who was allowed to come in or not. But they couldn't provide security because it was technically and physically impossible, because there were very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we can break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hadzic, you will be back on the witness stand tomorrow morning at 9.00 so you stay under oath. Thank you. Court adjourned.
